sections.title: Schedule II Partial Fills and the Massachusetts 30-Day Ceiling
sections.subtopic: Choosing the pathway, the clock, the record and the actor
learning_objectives: Distinguish a prohibited refill from a lawful remainder of a partial fill.
Choose the federal remainder clock by identifying which partial-fill pathway the facts trigger.
Apply the Massachusetts 30-day issue-date ceiling on top of whichever federal clock the pathway supplies.
Apply the Massachusetts five-day limit using the trigger the regulation actually states.
State what each actor must specify or record in each pathway.

orientation.text: A Schedule II prescription cannot be refilled. That single sentence causes most of the confusion in this area, because a partial fill looks like a refill from the counter: the patient comes back and leaves with more drug. The difference is that a refill is a fresh authorisation to dispense the full quantity again, while the remainder of a partial fill is the unfilled balance of the one quantity the prescriber already authorised. Nothing is created; something already authorised is completed. Getting that distinction right is what lets the rest of the area make sense.

Federal law then supplies three separate partial-fill pathways, and each carries its own clock. Where the pharmacy simply could not supply the full quantity, the remainder may be filled within 72 hours of the first partial filling, after which the prescriber must be notified and no further quantity may go out without a new prescription. Where the patient or the prescriber asked for a partial fill, the remainder runs to 30 days after the prescription was written -- except that an emergency oral prescription collapses that to 72 hours from issue. Where the patient is in a long-term care facility or has a documented terminal illness, partial filling may continue for up to 60 days from issue unless the medication is discontinued sooner. The first question on any partial-fill fact pattern is therefore never 'how long', it is 'which pathway', because the pathway picks the clock.

Massachusetts then puts a ceiling over all of it. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) provides without qualification that a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance. There is no long-term care or terminal-illness carve-out from that sentence. So the federal 60-day figure, which is a real and correctly stated federal outer limit, cannot be worked in Massachusetts past day 30: counting the day after issue as day one, as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs, on day 31 there is no longer a valid prescription for the pathway to operate on. A federal outer limit is a ceiling on federal authority. It is never a grant of state validity, and the 60-day answer belongs only to a question that asks what federal law alone permits.

Massachusetts also has its own partial-fill scheme, and it appears twice with two different triggers. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, keeps the remainder at the same pharmacy, requires a patient-record notation, closes the remainder at 30 days from issue, and imposes a five-day limit on the INITIAL partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to subsection (d) or (d1/2). 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same five-day limit but triggers it off something a pharmacist can actually see: whether the prescriber's address ON THE PRESCRIPTION is outside the Commonwealth, counted in calendar days. The regulation is the operational form of the statute's rule, and it is the one that decides the question at the counter.

Finally the records, which are where the actors separate. On the stock-shortage pathway the pharmacist notes the quantity supplied. On the request-based pathway the practitioner's part is conditional: a practitioner who wants the prescription partially filled specifies the quantity for each partial filling, and that specification then caps what the patient side may later ask for; where the request comes instead from the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney, nothing is required of the prescriber first. The pharmacist's notation follows whoever asked: the quantity dispensed where the prescriber asked on the prescription; 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill', with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials, where the prescriber authorized the partial fill in a later consultation; and who requested it and on what date, with the quantity dispensed, where the patient side asked. On the long-term care and terminal-illness pathway the notation is not clerical at all: a partially filled prescription that does not carry 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' is deemed by the regulation to have been filled in violation of the Act. Massachusetts adds a patient-record notation, made by the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee, and it puts a separate duty on the prescribing practitioner: a Schedule II opioid prescription must carry on its face the notation that the patient may request less than the full quantity.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts written oxycodone prescription for an LTCF resident is issued on 1 March and partially filled on 5 March under the federal long-term care pathway. On 12 April the facility asks for a further partial quantity. The prescription has not been discontinued and quantity remains authorised. Federal law would still allow it. May you dispense?
steps: Confirm the federal pathway is genuinely open. 12 April is day 42 from issue, inside the 60-day outer limit, and the medication has not been discontinued, so federal law does not stop you.
Now apply the Massachusetts ceiling. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 30 days after the date of issuance, without qualification.

Count the days as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs, with the day after issue as day one: 31 March is day 30, the last day inside the 30 days, and from 1 April the prescription is invalid. That was eleven days before the request, which fell on day 42.

Ask what the federal 60-day figure actually is. It is an outer limit on that federal pathway, not a grant of Massachusetts validity, so it cannot revive a prescription the state has already invalidated.
worked_examples.resolution: No. The prescription is dead in Massachusetts and a further partial dispensing would be made on an invalid prescription. The error this invites is answering 60 days because the question mentions an LTCF resident; 60 days is the right answer only where the question asks what federal law alone permits.

worked_examples.scenario: A patient presents a Schedule II prescription written by a Rhode Island prescriber whose address is printed on the prescription, issued six days ago, and asks for only part of the quantity. Your colleague says the five-day limit does not apply because nobody has established which statutory subsection the prescription came in under.
steps: Read the regulation rather than the statute. 105 CMR 721.055(A) attaches the five-day limit where the prescription was issued by a prescriber from a location other than the Commonwealth, as indicated by the address of the prescriber on the prescription.
That test is satisfied on its face here: the address printed on the prescription is out of state. No subsection adjudication is required.
Count in calendar days from the prescription issue date, which is what the regulation specifies. Six days is outside the limit.

Do not treat the limit as touching only the partial fill. Unless the Rhode Island prescriber also holds a registration under chapter 94C, the prescription was not issued under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(a), and it can be filled in Massachusetts only under s. 18(d), for a nonnarcotic Schedule II drug, or s. 18(d1/2), for a narcotic one from a practitioner registered in Maine or a contiguous state such as Rhode Island. Each of those subsections authorizes filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days.
So the 30-day Massachusetts validity period is not there to fall back on. On day six a prescription that depends on s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2) cannot be filled at all, in full or in part.
worked_examples.resolution: No fill of any kind can be made on these facts unless the prescriber also holds a Massachusetts registration. Even then, 105 CMR 721.055(A) bars the partial fill the patient asked for, because it keys off the out-of-state address on the prescription and six calendar days have passed; only a full fill within the 30-day validity period would remain. The colleague's test is the statute's; the regulation supplies an address-based trigger that the pharmacist can apply from the face of the prescription, and it is the operative one at the counter.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber writes a Schedule II prescription for 60 tablets and specifies on its face that it is to be partially filled in three dispensings of 20. After the first 20 are dispensed, the patient telephones and asks for 30 next time because they are going away. Your technician says a patient may request any quantity they like.
steps: Confirm the request route is valid. A patient may request a partial fill in person, in writing if signed, or by telephone, so the telephone call is not the problem.
Check whether the practitioner has already specified quantities. Here they specified 20 per filling on the face of the prescription under 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(3).
Apply the cap. Where the practitioner has requested partial filling in that way, the patient may not request a partial filling in an amount greater than the practitioner specified.
Keep the running total in view: across all partial fillings the total dispensed may not exceed the total quantity prescribed.
Record the request properly: the patient requested a partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed.
worked_examples.resolution: You may dispense up to 20, not 30. Going to 30 would need the prescriber to change the specification. The technician's rule is right, within the total prescribed, for a prescription the practitioner left unspecified, and wrong for this one.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Three federal partial-fill pathways, three clocks: stock shortage ______; requested partial fill ______; LTCF or terminal illness ______.
retrieval_prompts.answer: 72 hours from the first partial filling; 30 days from when the prescription was written (72 hours from issue if it was an emergency oral prescription); up to 60 days from the issue date.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why can a Massachusetts LTCF partial fill not run to 60 days?
retrieval_prompts.answer: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates a written or electronic Schedule II prescription 30 days after issuance with no LTCF or terminal-illness carve-out, and a federal outer limit is not a grant of state validity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the Massachusetts five-day partial-fill limit applies only once you have established that the prescription was filled under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2).
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 105 CMR 721.055(A) triggers it off the prescriber's address as it appears on the prescription, counted in calendar days.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A partially filled LTCF prescription does not carry the words 'LTCF patient' or 'terminally ill'. What follows?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The regulation deems it to have been filled in violation of the Act.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What four things must be recorded for EACH partial filling on the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The date of the partial filling, the quantity dispensed, the remaining quantity authorised to be dispensed, and the identification of the dispensing pharmacist.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where the practitioner has already specified per-fill quantities, may the patient request a larger partial fill?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. A patient, a minor's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's named caregiver may not request more than the practitioner specified.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: a patient may ask for a partial fill of a Schedule II prescription only if the practitioner specified per-fill quantities on it.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. The per-fill specification is owed only where the practitioner wants the prescription partially filled. The patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney may ask without it, and in Massachusetts the pharmacist must then dispense the lesser quantity.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A prescriber specified on a Schedule II prescription, when issuing it, that it be dispensed in two partial fillings. What does the pharmacist note at the first one?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The quantity dispensed, on the face of the written prescription or in the electronic record, and the pharmacy keeps the dispensing record. 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' is for a partial fill the prescriber authorized later in a consultation, and the requester-and-date entry is for a patient-side request.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: In Massachusetts, is dispensing a lesser quantity on patient request permitted or required?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Required. The pharmacist shall dispense the lesser quantity if the patient requests it.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Where must the Schedule II opioid partial-fill notation appear, and who puts it there?
retrieval_prompts.answer: On the prescription itself: M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) makes it part of what the prescribing practitioner must include when issuing a Schedule II opioid prescription. It is a different thing from the patient-record notation the pharmacist or designee makes at each partial dispensing.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: On federal law alone, may a second pharmacy dispense the remaining portion of a partially filled Schedule II prescription?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) transfers an electronic prescription only for its initial dispensing and 21 CFR 1306.25 moves only Schedule III-V prescription information for refills; DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits a partially filled prescription to be transferred for the remaining portion. Massachusetts reaches the same result expressly in s. 18(d3/4).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule II prescription from a Rhode Island prescriber who holds no Massachusetts registration is presented six days after issue. May it be filled in full instead of in part?
retrieval_prompts.answer: No. Such a prescription is fillable in Massachusetts only under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), and each authorizes filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days.

quick_review.text: A Schedule II prescription may not be refilled; dispensing a lawful unfilled remainder of a partial fill is not a refill.

Federal law supplies three partial-fill pathways with three different remainder clocks: 72 hours when the pharmacy could not supply the full quantity, 30 days from the writing date when the patient or prescriber requested the partial fill, and up to 60 days from issue for an LTCF resident or a terminally ill patient.

In Massachusetts a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a), so no federal pathway can be worked past day 30 on that prescription.

M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, keeps the remaining portion at the same pharmacy, requires a patient-record notation of the partial fill and quantity, and requires the remaining portion to be filled not later than 30 days after the prescription issue date. Federal law gives no route to move the remaining portion to another pharmacy either.

105 CMR 721.055(A) states the five-day initial partial-fill limit with an address-based trigger: it applies where the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth, counted in calendar days from issue.

A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner who is not registered under M.G.L. c. 94C can be filled in Massachusetts only under s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), and only if it was issued within the preceding five days, whether the fill is full or partial.

Every federal partial fill carries a notation duty of its own. A practitioner who wants a request-based partial fill specifies the per-fill quantities, and a patient-side request then cannot exceed them; a request by the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney needs no prior specification. On the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway a partially filled prescription lacking the 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' notation is deemed filled in violation of the Act.

The prescribing practitioner must include on a Massachusetts prescription for a Schedule II opioid a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

decision_logic.condition: The original Schedule II quantity was fully dispensed.
decision_logic.action: Do not process an additional dispensing as a refill; require a new lawful prescription unless a distinct pathway applies.

decision_logic.condition: The pharmacy could not supply the full Schedule II quantity.
decision_logic.action: Note the quantity supplied on the prescription record, then use the 72-hour remainder rule; past 72 hours notify the prescriber and obtain a new prescription for any further quantity.

decision_logic.condition: The patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney, or the prescriber requested a partial fill of a written or electronic Schedule II prescription, and state law does not prohibit it.
decision_logic.action: If the practitioner specified per-fill quantities, keep any patient-side request within them; make the notation that fits the requester (the quantity dispensed for a request made on the prescription, 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' with the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials for one made in consultation, or the requester and the date of the request with the quantity dispensed for a patient-side request); keep the dispensing record; and complete any remainder no later than 30 days after the prescription was written.

decision_logic.condition: The patient or prescriber requested a partial fill of an emergency oral Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Complete any remainder no later than 72 hours after the prescription was issued; the ordinary 30-day request-based period does not reach an emergency oral prescription.

decision_logic.condition: The Schedule II prescription is for an LTCF resident or a patient with a documented terminal illness.
decision_logic.action: Record 'LTCF patient' or 'terminally ill' on the prescription before partially filling it, contact the practitioner first if terminal status is uncertain, and log the date, quantity dispensed, remaining quantity authorised and dispensing pharmacist for each partial filling.

decision_logic.condition: The prescriber's address printed on a Schedule II prescription is outside Massachusetts.
decision_logic.action: The prescription must be presented for initial partial fill not later than five calendar days after its issue date.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner who is not registered under M.G.L. c. 94C is presented more than five days after issue.
decision_logic.action: Do not fill it at all, in full or in part: s. 18(d) and s. 18(d1/2) authorize filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days.

decision_logic.condition: The federal pathway you selected would allow a further partial dispensing more than 30 days after the Massachusetts written or electronic Schedule II prescription was issued.
decision_logic.action: Stop. The prescription is already invalid in Massachusetts under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a); the federal outer limit is a ceiling on federal authority and does not extend Massachusetts validity.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts patient requests a lesser quantity of a Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Dispense the lesser quantity, note the partial fill and quantity in the patient record accessible to the prescriber on request, keep any remainder at the same pharmacy, and fill it not later than 30 days after the issue date.

decision_logic.condition: The patient asks a different pharmacy to dispense the remaining portion of a partially filled Schedule II prescription.
decision_logic.action: Decline: under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) only the pharmacy that dispensed the lesser quantity may dispense the remaining portion, and no federal transfer pathway moves a partially filled prescription to a second pharmacy.

ma_vs_federal.text: 21 CFR 1306.13(c) allows LTCF and terminal-illness Schedule II partial fills for up to 60 days from issue, but M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidates the written or electronic prescription 30 days after issuance. Both apply, so in Massachusetts the working outer limit is 30 days and the federal 60-day figure answers only a question about federal law alone.

Federal request-based partial filling is permissive, and among its conditions are that the partial fill is not prohibited by State law and that the prescription is written and filled in accordance with State law; M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) goes further and makes the lesser-quantity dispensing mandatory on patient request, and adds a patient-record notation and a 30-day issue-date deadline of its own for the remaining portion.

Both sovereigns keep the remaining portion at the pharmacy that made the partial fill. Massachusetts says so expressly in s. 18(d3/4); federally no transfer pathway reaches a partially filled prescription, because 21 CFR 1306.08(e) is for initial dispensing and 21 CFR 1306.25 for Schedule III-V refills, and DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits the remaining portion to be transferred.
Partial-fill notation is not a Massachusetts-only duty: 21 CFR 1306.13(a) and (b)(5) impose federal notation and dispensing-record duties that run alongside the Massachusetts patient-record notation.

exceptions.text: The 72-hour remainder rule is tied to the pharmacy's inability to supply the full quantity and is not a substitute for the request-based pathway.

The request-based 30-day remainder period carries its own emergency-oral exception: the remainder of a partially filled emergency oral Schedule II prescription must be filled no later than 72 hours after the prescription is issued.
The 60-day LTCF and terminal-illness period is an outer limit on that federal pathway, not an extension of any state validity period, and it ends earlier if the medication is discontinued.

The five-day initial partial-dispensing limit in M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) reaches only a prescription filled under subsection (d) or (d1/2) -- respectively a nonnarcotic Schedule II prescription from an out-of-state practitioner and a narcotic Schedule II prescription from a practitioner registered in Maine or a state contiguous with the commonwealth -- and not every patient-requested partial fill. Those two subsections also authorize filling only of prescriptions issued within the preceding five days, so a prescription that depends on them cannot be filled at all after that point, in full or in part; their other conditions belong to the out-of-state pathway.

Where the practitioner has specified per-fill quantities in advance, a patient-side request may not exceed them, and no pathway permits the total across all partial fillings to exceed the total quantity prescribed.
The day-counting rule in 247 CMR 9.04(10) is one of the requirements 247 CMR 9.04(15) disapplies at institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

timing_deadlines.consequence: Otherwise notify the prescriber; no further quantity may be supplied beyond 72 hours without a new prescription.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: No later than 30 days after the prescription was written
timing_deadlines.consequence: The remaining portion cannot be dispensed after the deadline.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: No later than 72 hours after the prescription is issued
timing_deadlines.consequence: The emergency oral remainder cannot use the ordinary 30-day request-based period.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Up to 60 days from the issue date unless discontinued sooner
timing_deadlines.consequence: The federal outer limit on the pathway; correct only where the question asks what federal law alone permits.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: 30 days after the date of issuance
timing_deadlines.consequence: The prescription becomes invalid, so no partial dispensing may be made after day 30, counting the day after issue as day one, even though federal law would have allowed 60.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Not later than 5 calendar days after the prescription issue date
timing_deadlines.consequence: The prescription can no longer be presented for an initial partial fill.

timing_deadlines.timeframe: Only if the prescription was issued within the preceding 5 days
timing_deadlines.consequence: After that point neither subsection authorizes filling the prescription, in full or in part.

forms_records.text: On the stock-shortage pathway the pharmacist notes the quantity supplied on the face of the written prescription, in the written record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record.

On the request-based pathway the notation follows whoever asked. Where the prescriber asked for partial filling on the prescription when issuing it, having specified the quantity for each partial filling, the pharmacist notes the quantity dispensed on the face of the written prescription or in the pharmacy's electronic records, in the record of the emergency oral prescription, or in the electronic prescription record. Where the prescriber authorized a later partial fill in a consultation, the pharmacist notes 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill', the practitioner's name, the date and time of the discussion and the pharmacist's initials. Where the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney asked, no prior specification is needed, and the pharmacist notes that that person requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed.

Each request-based partial filling also generates a dispensing record carrying the date, the name or initials of the person who dispensed, and the elements 21 CFR 1306.22(c) requires for Schedule III and IV refills; for an electronic prescription that information must be linked to the electronic prescription record.

On the LTCF or terminal-illness pathway the pharmacist records 'terminally ill' or 'LTCF patient' on the prescription itself, and for each partial filling records the date, the quantity dispensed, the remaining quantity authorised and the dispensing pharmacist's identification.

Massachusetts adds a notation of each partial dispensing and its quantity in the pharmacy patient record, made by the pharmacist or the pharmacist's designee and accessible to the prescribing practitioner on request, whether the dispensing is the initial partial fill or the remaining portion.

The prescribing practitioner must include on a Massachusetts prescription for a Schedule II opioid the notation under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity. It is part of the prescription's content, separate from the pharmacist's patient-record notation.

role_duties.duty: Identify the factual trigger for the partial fill before selecting any deadline, because the three federal pathways carry three different clocks.

Where the practitioner wants a Schedule II prescription partially filled, specify the quantity to be dispensed in each partial filling on the prescription when it is signed, or authorize a later partial fill after consultation with a pharmacist, and keep the total within the quantity prescribed. A partial fill requested by the patient, a minor patient's parent or legal guardian, or an adult patient's caregiver named in a medical power of attorney requires nothing of the prescriber first.
Include on every Massachusetts Schedule II opioid prescription the notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity.

Make the partial-fill notation that fits the requester and keep the dispensing record for each request-based partial filling: the quantity dispensed where the prescriber asked on the prescription, the 'Authorized by Practitioner to Partial Fill' entry after a consultation, and the requester and date, with the quantity, for a patient-side request.
Check the Massachusetts issue-date ceiling before dispensing any remainder, since a federal pathway that is still open may sit on a prescription Massachusetts has already invalidated.
Dispense the lesser quantity when a Massachusetts patient requests a partial fill of a Schedule II prescription; that dispensing is mandatory rather than discretionary.

Contact the practitioner before partially filling where it is unclear whether the patient may be classified as terminally ill; the responsibility to assure the substance is for a terminally ill patient is shared with the prescriber.

common_traps.text: Calling every later Schedule II dispensing a refill erases the lawful partial-fill remainder distinction.
Choosing 72 hours whenever a Schedule II prescription is partial ignores who requested the partial fill and why.
Carrying the federal 60-day figure into a Massachusetts scenario dispenses a Schedule II drug on a prescription that M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) invalidated on day 31.
Reading the Massachusetts patient-requested partial fill as an option the pharmacist may decline turns a mandatory duty into a permission.
Looking for the statutory subsection before applying the five-day limit misses that the regulation triggers it off the prescriber's address printed on the prescription.
Treating the LTCF or terminal-illness notation as clerical overlooks that a partially filled prescription without it is deemed filled in violation of the Act.
Assuming a patient may request any partial quantity ignores the cap a practitioner's advance specification imposes.
Turning away a patient's partial-fill request because the prescriber specified no per-fill quantities treats a condition of the prescriber's own request as a condition of the patient's.

sections.title: Schedule III-V Refills and Massachusetts Transfers
learning_objectives: Apply both the issue-date clock and refill-count limit to Schedule III and IV prescriptions.
Separate transfer eligibility from the prescription's remaining lawful refill capacity.
Recognize the special Massachusetts treatment of Schedule VI transfers.
Separate the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer from the Massachusetts duty to transfer at the patient's request.
Identify who may execute a transfer, and separate the initial-dispensing electronic transfer from the refill-purpose transfer.

orientation.text: A refillable controlled prescription carries two separate ceilings, and both must be checked before every dispensing. One is a count of refills; the other is a clock that runs from the date the practitioner issued the prescription, not from the day the pharmacy first dispensed it. In Massachusetts the count itself follows 247 CMR 9.04(10): to decide whether a prescription is within date, the pharmacist counts the day after the prescription was written as day one. Federal law sets both for Schedules III and IV in a single sentence: no such prescription may be filled or refilled more than six months after the issue date, and no such prescription authorized to be refilled may be refilled more than five times. The word 'filled' matters. The six-month bar is not a limit on refills alone; a prescription that has never been dispensed at all is equally out of time once six months have passed. The two ceilings are also independent rather than cumulative, so a prescription with four unused refills and a seven-month-old issue date is exhausted, and a prescription two months old that has already been refilled five times is exhausted too. Neither ceiling is lifted by anything the pharmacy does; the practitioner must renew the therapy on a new prescription.

Massachusetts contributes the schedule the federal refill provision leaves out. 21 CFR 1306.22 is written for Schedules III and IV, and it does not supply refill limits for Schedule V. 247 CMR 9.04(13) fills that space with the same pair of numbers and the same structure: a licensee may not fill or refill a Schedule V prescription more than six months after the date it was issued, and a Schedule V prescription may not be refilled more than five times. Because the state provision borrows the federal shape, candidates often recall the figures correctly but attribute them to the wrong sovereign; on a Massachusetts Schedule V question the authority is the state regulation. That subsection also carries a facility-scope limit the federal rule has no counterpart to: 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies, and the same provision also reaches the counting rule in 9.04(10) and the Schedule VI rule in 9.04(12). The exclusion removes those state subsections from that facility type; it does not disapply any other body of law that may reach the same dispensing.

Transfer is a different question from refill capacity, and confusing the two is the most productive error in this area. A transfer moves an existing prescription from one pharmacy to another. It does not create refill authority, and it does not restart the issue-date clock; the prescription arrives at the receiving pharmacy with exactly the refills and the issue date it already had. What Massachusetts adds is a duty on the pharmacy rather than a limit on the prescription. Under 247 CMR 9.14, a pharmacy shall transfer a prescription to another pharmacy at the request of a patient or the patient's agent, in a timely manner so as not to delay patient therapy; the pharmacy may act as the patient's agent in order to facilitate the transfer; and a pharmacy may not charge a fee for transferring a prescription. That trio is a consumer-protection layer. It answers whether the pharmacy must move the prescription, who does the legwork, and what it may cost the patient. It says nothing at all about how many transfers the prescription itself is entitled to.

That second question is federal. 21 CFR 1306.25(a) permits the transfer of original prescription information for a Schedule III, IV or V controlled substance for the purpose of refill dispensing between pharmacies on a one-time basis only. The single circumstance that changes the number is a shared record: pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization. The structure follows the concern. Each hand-off between two separate recordkeeping systems is a seam where a prescription could be dispensed twice, which is why the transferring pharmacist voids the original and the receiving pharmacist records where it came from and how many refills survive; where both pharmacies read and write the same live record, that seam does not exist and the cap is unnecessary. The two sovereigns then stack in one direction only. 21 CFR 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure permissible only if allowable under existing State or other applicable law, so a state may withhold transfers the federal rule would permit. Nothing runs the other way: a state duty to transfer does not manufacture federal transfer capacity, so the Massachusetts obligation operates within the one-time cap rather than over it.

Massachusetts Schedule VI sits outside that federal cap entirely, and the reason lies in how Massachusetts builds its schedules. M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a) directs that the first five Massachusetts schedules incorporate the federal ones, and 105 CMR 700.002(A) through (E) define them as the substances listed in 21 CFR 1308.11 through 1308.15; 105 CMR 700.002(F) then places in Schedule VI all prescription drugs not included in any other schedule. 21 CFR 1306.25 reaches substances listed in federal Schedules III through V, which are the substances Massachusetts places in its own Schedules III through V, so it does not reach a Schedule VI drug. (Section 2(a1/2) also requires a substance newly controlled under federal law to be placed in a corresponding Massachusetts schedule within 30 days of the federal notice.) The state regulation governs alone, and it is more generous than the federal rule it borrows its procedure from: 247 CMR 9.14(4)(a) directs that Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedules III through V prescriptions, 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, and 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued. Read together, the Schedule VI transfer limit is a count of refills bounded by an age, not a count of transfers. The same one-year clock governs refilling. Under 247 CMR 9.04(12) a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f) allows a refill only where the original prescription provides for refilling and specifies the number of refills; that section reaches Schedule VI because s. 1 defines a controlled substance as one in any schedule the chapter refers to. Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no refills left and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, 9.04(12) lets the pharmacist, in professional judgment, dispense up to a 14-day supply or the smallest available unit-of-use package. Do not import the five-refill and six-month figures from Schedules III through V into a Schedule VI prescription.

Finally, federal law offers two transfer pathways, not one, and they are told apart by whether the prescription has ever been dispensed. 21 CFR 1306.25 is the refill-purpose pathway just described: it presupposes a prescription with refills remaining, reaches Schedules III through V, and carries the shared-database allowance. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) is separate. It permits the transfer for initial dispensing of an electronic controlled-substance prescription between retail pharmacies, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V. Where the prescription transferred on this pathway is a Schedule III, IV or V substance and includes authorized refills, those refills travel with the initial prescription to the receiving pharmacy. The pathway is narrow in the ways the refill-purpose rule is not: the prescription must stay in electronic form and must not be altered, and there is no shared-database counterpart, so it remains available once, whatever database the two pharmacies share. Both federal pathways require the transfer to be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, and both are permissible only where state law allows the transfer. That pharmacist-to-pharmacist requirement is why the Massachusetts allowance in 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) for a certified pharmacy technician to perform prescription transfers, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty, is confined to Schedule VI, where no federal pathway operates.

worked_examples.scenario: A Schedule IV prescription was issued on 1 March authorizing five refills. The patient first had it dispensed on 5 March and used three refills at Pharmacy A. On 20 August she asks Pharmacy B to obtain it, and the transfer is completed on 22 August. On 10 September she asks Pharmacy B for the next refill. May Pharmacy B dispense it?
steps: Start with the two ceilings. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) bars filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after the date on which it was issued, so the window closes six months after 1 March. Counted the Massachusetts way, the day after issue is day one (247 CMR 9.04(10)), so 1 March itself is not counted.
Count the refills separately. Three of the five authorized refills have been used, so two remain and the five-refill ceiling is not the obstacle in this fact pattern.

Ask what the 22 August transfer changed. It moved the prescription without creating new refill authority and without restarting the issue-date clock, so the prescription reached Pharmacy B carrying the same 1 March issue date and the same two remaining refills.
Apply the clock on 10 September. The six-month period measured from 1 March has run, and unused authorized refills do not survive the time limit.
worked_examples.resolution: Pharmacy B may not dispense the refill; only a new prescription from the practitioner restores capacity. The scenario invites two errors at once: starting the six months at the 5 March first dispensing, and treating the two unused refills as authority that outlives the clock.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts patient's Schedule III prescription with refills remaining was transferred from Pharmacy A to Pharmacy B last month. She now asks Pharmacy C to obtain it from Pharmacy B, and mentions that Pharmacy B told her it would charge five dollars to send it and that she would have to telephone Pharmacy B herself. Pharmacies B and C do not share a prescription database.
steps: Identify the pathway. The prescription has already been dispensed and has refills remaining, so this is a refill-purpose transfer under 21 CFR 1306.25 rather than the initial-dispensing electronic transfer.

Apply the federal ceiling before the state duty. 1306.25(a) permits the refill-purpose transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information on a one-time basis only, and that transfer has already been used moving the prescription from A to B.

Test the exception. It is available only where the pharmacies electronically share a real-time, online database. B and C do not, so the alternative allowing transfer up to the maximum authorized refills is unavailable.

Do not read the Massachusetts duty as an override. 247 CMR 9.14(1) says when a pharmacy must transfer; 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure permissible only if allowable under state law, so state law can withhold a federally permitted transfer but cannot supply federal transfer capacity the federal rule withholds.

Separate the two complaints the patient actually raised. The fee and the legwork are governed by 247 CMR 9.14(3) and 9.14(2), which forbid a transfer fee and permit the pharmacy to act as the patient's agent; those rules are unaffected by the transfer count.
worked_examples.resolution: The second refill-purpose transfer is not available on these facts, and a new prescription is what moves the therapy to Pharmacy C. The five-dollar charge and the instruction that the patient make her own telephone call were both improper regardless. The trap is reading the Massachusetts duty to transfer on request as removing the federal one-time cap.

worked_examples.scenario: A Massachusetts patient asks Pharmacy C to obtain a Schedule VI prescription issued eight months ago with four refills remaining. It has already been transferred once, from Pharmacy A to Pharmacy B. Pharmacy C has a certified pharmacy technician on shift and the pharmacist on duty approves her doing the work. A colleague objects that the federal one-time limit forbids a second transfer and that only a pharmacist may execute one.
steps: Classify the drug first. Massachusetts Schedules I through V are the substances the federal schedules list (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a); 105 CMR 700.002(A)-(E)), and 105 CMR 700.002(F) puts in Schedule VI only prescription drugs included in no other schedule. A Schedule VI drug is therefore not one of the substances the federal Schedules III, IV and V list.

That settles the first objection. 21 CFR 1306.25 governs the transfer of Schedule III, IV and V prescription information, so it never reaches this prescription and its one-time cap has nothing here to limit.

Apply the state rule that does govern. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(a) puts a Schedule VI transfer on the same footing as a Schedule III-V transfer, and 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum number of remaining refills authorized by the prescriber, which is a count of refills rather than a count of transfers.

Check the state ceilings that do exist. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(c) bars transferring a Schedule VI prescription authorizing refills more than one year from the date it was issued, and eight months is inside that period. The refills themselves are also still usable, because 247 CMR 9.04(12) keeps a Schedule VI prescription valid, and refillable, for one year from issue.

Now the second objection. The federal requirement that a transfer be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists belongs to the federal pathways, which do not reach this prescription, and 247 CMR 8.04(4)(d) permits a certified pharmacy technician to perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.
worked_examples.resolution: Both halves of the colleague's objection fail: the second transfer is permitted and the technician may execute it with the pharmacist's approval. The error the scenario invites is carrying a federal Schedule III-V mechanic across to a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription that no federal schedule reaches.

worked_examples.scenario: A prescriber transmits an electronic Schedule II prescription to retail Pharmacy A. The drug is out of stock and nothing has been dispensed. The patient asks Pharmacy A to send the prescription to retail Pharmacy B. A technician offers to print it and fax it across, and a colleague says a Schedule II prescription can never be moved between pharmacies.
steps: Rule out the wrong pathway. 21 CFR 1306.25 transfers prescription information for the purpose of refill dispensing, and this prescription has never been dispensed, so that rule is not the one in play.

Identify the right one. 21 CFR 1306.08(e) permits the transfer for initial dispensing of an electronic controlled-substance prescription between retail pharmacies, upon request from the patient, on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V.
Refuse the print-and-fax. The pathway requires the prescription to remain in electronic form and unaltered; converting it to another form defeats the transfer.

Refuse the technician's participation on this transfer. The federal pathway requires the transfer to be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, and the Massachusetts certified-technician transfer authority is confined to Schedule VI in any event.
Note what is not available here. This pathway carries no shared-database counterpart, so it stays one-time regardless of what record system the two pharmacies share.
worked_examples.resolution: The transfer is lawful, but only electronically, pharmacist to pharmacist, and once. The colleague's flat rule is the error the scenario invites; a never-dispensed electronic Schedule II prescription has a transfer pathway even though the refill-transfer rule does not reach Schedule II.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Schedule III or IV prescription may not be filled or refilled more than ______ after the date it was issued, and may not be refilled more than ______ times.
retrieval_prompts.answer: six months; five. Both limits are in 21 CFR 1306.22(a), and each is independent of the other.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Which sovereign supplies the five-refill and six-month limits for a Schedule V prescription, and which facility type is excluded from them?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Massachusetts, at 247 CMR 9.04(13); the federal refill provision at 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is written for Schedules III and IV. 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that 9.04(13) does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: the six-month clock starts running at the first dispensing, and it limits refills only.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False on both counts. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) and 247 CMR 9.04(13) each measure from the date the prescription was issued, and each bars filling as well as refilling once six months have passed, so a prescription that has never been dispensed is equally out of time. In Massachusetts the day after the prescription was written counts as day one (247 CMR 9.04(10)).

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How many times may Schedule III-V prescription information be transferred for refill purposes, and what single circumstance changes that number?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Once. Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may instead transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A patient asks a retail pharmacy to move a never-dispensed electronic Schedule II prescription to another retail pharmacy. Which pathway applies, and does the shared-database allowance help?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The initial-dispensing electronic transfer under 21 CFR 1306.08(e), which reaches Schedules II through V. No: that pathway has no shared-database counterpart and stays one-time, and the prescription must remain electronic and unaltered.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: True or false: because Massachusetts requires a pharmacy to transfer on the patient's request, a Schedule IV prescription that has already been transferred once may be transferred again.
retrieval_prompts.answer: False. 247 CMR 9.14(1) says when a transfer must happen; 21 CFR 1306.25(a) says how many are available, and 1306.25(e) makes the federal procedure turn on state law permitting transfers rather than the reverse. Absent a shared real-time, online database, the second transfer is unavailable.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Why does the federal one-time refill-transfer limit not cap a Massachusetts Schedule VI transfer, and what state ceiling applies instead?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Because Massachusetts Schedules I-V are the substances the federal schedules list (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 2(a); 105 CMR 700.002(A)-(E)) and Schedule VI holds only prescription drugs in none of them (700.002(F)), so a Schedule VI drug is not a federal Schedule III-V substance and 21 CFR 1306.25 does not reach it. 247 CMR 9.14(4)(b) permits transfer up to the maximum remaining refills the prescriber authorized, and 9.14(4)(c) bars transfer of a refill-authorizing Schedule VI prescription more than one year after issue.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: A Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription issued 13 months ago still shows two refills, and the prescriber cannot be reached today. May it be refilled, and what may the pharmacist do?
retrieval_prompts.answer: It may not be refilled: under 247 CMR 9.04(12) a Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from the date of issue and may not be refilled after one year. Because prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use package.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: Who may execute a prescription transfer, federally and in Massachusetts?
retrieval_prompts.answer: Federally, the transfer must be communicated directly between two licensed pharmacists, on both the refill-purpose pathway and the initial-dispensing electronic pathway. Massachusetts adds that a certified pharmacy technician may perform prescription transfers between pharmacies for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: What must the transferring and receiving pharmacists record on a refill-purpose transfer of a Schedule III-V prescription, and how long are the records kept?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The transferring pharmacist writes 'VOID' on the prescription (or marks the electronic record as transferred) and records the receiving pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the receiving pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name. The receiving pharmacist records the prescription's history (issue date, refills authorized and remaining, dates and locations of earlier fills, and the transferring and originally filling pharmacies), writing 'transfer' on the face of a paper or oral prescription or creating an electronic record for an electronic one. The original and transferred prescriptions are kept for two years from the date of last refill.

retrieval_prompts.prompt: How does a Massachusetts pharmacist count days when deciding whether a prescription is within date?
retrieval_prompts.answer: The day after the prescription was written is day one (247 CMR 9.04(10)); the issue date itself is not counted. 247 CMR 9.04(15) disapplies this counting rule at institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

quick_review.text: Federal law bars filling or refilling a Schedule III or IV prescription more than six months after the issue date and bars more than five refills; only a new prescription lifts either limit.

For pharmacies subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13), a Massachusetts Schedule V prescription may not be filled or refilled more than six months after issue, and may not be refilled more than five times; that subsection does not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

For pharmacies subject to 247 CMR 9.04(12), a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription is valid for one year from issue and may not be refilled after one year, and any refill needs the original prescription to provide for refilling and state the number of refills (M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f)).
At a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(10), the day after the prescription was written is day one when deciding whether it is within date.
Massachusetts requires a timely patient-requested transfer, prohibits a transfer fee, and permits a pharmacy to act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer.

Transfer of Schedule III-V prescription information for refill purposes is permitted between pharmacies on a one-time basis only, unless the pharmacies electronically share a real-time, online database.

Transfer of an unfilled electronic controlled-substance prescription for initial dispensing is a separate federal pathway, permitted between retail pharmacies at the patient's request on a one-time basis only, and it reaches Schedules II through V.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule III or IV refill is requested.
decision_logic.action: Check both elapsed time from issue and the number of prior refills; either exhausted limit blocks the refill.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts Schedule V refill is requested at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(13).
decision_logic.action: Apply the five-refill and six-month limits independently.

decision_logic.condition: A Massachusetts Schedule VI refill is requested at a pharmacy subject to 247 CMR 9.04(12).
decision_logic.action: Confirm the original prescription provides for refills and states their number, and that it is within one year of issue. Past one year, or with no refills left, dispense only a professional-judgment supply of up to 14 days or the smallest unit-of-use package, and only if prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in time.

decision_logic.condition: The facility is an institutional sterile compounding pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Do not apply the Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13), the Schedule VI rule in 9.04(12) or the counting rule in 9.04(10) through those provisions; 247 CMR 9.04(15) excludes that facility type.

decision_logic.condition: A patient or authorized agent requests a Massachusetts prescription transfer.
decision_logic.action: Transfer remaining authorized refills timely without charging a transfer fee, subject to the prescription-specific limits.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks to move a Schedule III, IV or V prescription with authorized refills remaining to another pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Confirm the prescription has not already been transferred once, unless the two pharmacies electronically share a real-time online database, before applying the Massachusetts transfer duty.

decision_logic.condition: A patient asks a retail pharmacy to move an ELECTRONIC controlled-substance prescription that has never been dispensed to another retail pharmacy.
decision_logic.action: Use the initial-dispensing electronic transfer pathway rather than the refill-transfer rule, keep the prescription in electronic form and unaltered, and treat it as available once only. A never-dispensed paper prescription has no federal transfer pathway.

decision_logic.condition: A Schedule III-V prescription is transferred for refill purposes.
decision_logic.action: The transferring pharmacist voids the prescription and records where it went; the receiving pharmacist records the prescription's transfer history, writing 'transfer' on the face of a paper or oral prescription or creating an electronic record for an electronic one; the original and transferred prescriptions are kept for two years from the date of last refill.

ma_vs_federal.text: For Schedule III and IV refills the federal five-refill and six-month limits remain operative when the Massachusetts transfer rules are applied, and so does the separate federal limit permitting a Schedule III-V refill-purpose transfer only once.

Massachusetts Schedule VI prescriptions transfer in the same manner as Schedule III-V prescriptions and may move up to the maximum number of remaining refills the prescriber authorized, with the only ceiling being that a refill-authorising Schedule VI prescription may not be transferred more than one year after issue. The federal one-time limit does not cap them, because it reaches only substances in federal Schedules III-V, which Massachusetts places in its own Schedules III-V, while Schedule VI holds prescription drugs included in none of the other schedules.

For Schedule VI the refill limits come from Massachusetts: 247 CMR 9.04(12) makes the prescription valid for one year and bars refills after that, and M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(f) requires the original prescription to provide for and number any refill. The Schedule III-V figures of five refills and six months do not carry across.

A federal controlled-prescription transfer must pass directly between two licensed pharmacists, while Massachusetts lets a certified pharmacy technician do the work for Schedule VI only, with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.

exceptions.text: A transfer does not create new refill authority or restart an issue-date clock.
The Schedule V refill limits in 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies under 247 CMR 9.04(15).
247 CMR 9.04(15) also removes the Schedule VI rule in 9.04(12) and the day-counting rule in 9.04(10) from institutional sterile compounding pharmacies.

Where a Schedule VI prescription has expired or has no remaining refills and prescriber authorization cannot be obtained in a timely manner, the pharmacist may, in professional judgment, dispense a quantity not exceeding 14 days or the smallest available unit-of-use package; that is not an ordinary refill.
Pharmacies electronically sharing a real-time, online database may transfer up to the maximum refills permitted by law and the prescriber's authorization instead of the one-time limit.
The real-time shared-database allowance belongs to the refill-purpose transfer rule; the initial-dispensing electronic transfer carries no such counterpart and stays one-time.

The initial-dispensing transfer in 21 CFR 1306.08(e) is for a prescription's first dispensing. Once a Schedule II prescription has been partially filled, no federal transfer pathway moves its remaining portion to another pharmacy.

forms_records.text: On a refill-purpose transfer the transferring pharmacist writes 'VOID' on the face of the invalidated prescription (for an electronic prescription, adds to its record that it has been transferred), records the name, address and DEA registration number of the pharmacy it went to and the name of the receiving pharmacist, and records the date of the transfer and his or her own name.

For a paper prescription, or an oral one reduced to writing, the receiving pharmacist writes 'transfer' on its face, reduces to writing all the information a prescription must contain, and adds the original issue date, the original number of refills authorized, the date of original dispensing, the valid refills remaining with the dates and locations of previous refills, the transferring pharmacy's name, address, DEA registration number and prescription number, the transferring pharmacist's name, and the name, address, DEA registration number and prescription number of the pharmacy that originally filled it. For an electronic prescription transferred electronically, the transferring pharmacist sends that history with the prescription, and the receiving pharmacist creates an electronic record containing it and his or her own name.

The original and transferred prescriptions are kept for two years from the date of last refill, and pharmacies that share one electronic prescription record must still meet every information requirement of a manual transfer.

On an initial-dispensing electronic transfer the transferring pharmacist adds to the electronic record that it has been transferred, the receiving pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the receiving pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name; the receiving pharmacist adds 'transfer', the transferring pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the transferring pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name. Software may fill in these fields, but the pharmacist must ensure they are complete and accurate, and both pharmacies keep the records for two years from the date of the transfer.

role_duties.duty: Record the federal transfer data: on a paper or oral prescription, 'transfer' on its face with the full prescription information and transfer history; on an electronic refill transfer, an electronic record with the receiving pharmacist's name and everything transferred; on an initial-dispensing transfer, the entries the electronic-transfer rule lists. The prescription keeps the refills and the issue date it already had.

Transfer the prescription at the request of the patient or the patient's agent in a timely manner so as not to delay therapy, without charging a fee; on a Schedule III-V refill transfer, the transferring pharmacist writes 'VOID' on the prescription (or marks the electronic record as transferred) and records the receiving pharmacy's name, address and DEA registration number, the receiving pharmacist's name, the date and his or her own name.
May act as the patient's agent to obtain the transfer. This is a permission; the duty to transfer rests on the pharmacy asked to send the prescription.
Communicate a federal controlled-prescription transfer directly between the two of them; the transfer is a pharmacist-to-pharmacist act.
Perform a prescription transfer only for Schedule VI, and only with the approval of the pharmacist on duty.
Keep the transfer records for two years: from the date of last refill on a refill-purpose transfer, and from the date of transfer, at both pharmacies, on an initial-dispensing electronic transfer.

common_traps.text: Starting a six-month clock at the first dispensing rather than the issue date gives the prescription excess life.
Assuming a transfer renews or expands refill authority confuses movement of a prescription with creation of a new prescription.
Treating the Massachusetts duty to transfer on patient request as removing the federal one-time limit on a Schedule III-V refill transfer.
Concluding that a Schedule II prescription can never move between pharmacies overlooks the one-time initial-dispensing transfer of an unfilled electronic prescription.
Letting a certified pharmacy technician transfer a Schedule III-V prescription ignores both the Schedule VI limit on that authority and the federal pharmacist-to-pharmacist requirement.
Reading the Massachusetts Schedule V six-month limit as reaching only refills would let a seven-month-old prescription be dispensed for the first time.
Carrying the federal one-time transfer limit across to a Massachusetts Schedule VI prescription refuses a second transfer the regulation allows.
Treating the Schedule VI one-year figure as a transfer bar only lets a prescription be refilled after 247 CMR 9.04(12) has ended its validity.

Sending a partially filled Schedule II prescription through the initial-dispensing transfer overlooks that the pathway is for a prescription's first dispensing, and that no federal pathway moves the remaining portion.

sections.title: Federal and Massachusetts Rule Interaction
learning_objectives: Solve a federal-state interaction by identifying the same actor, event, and prescription pathway under both sources.
Avoid selecting a familiar federal limit before checking Massachusetts conditions that also govern the transaction.

orientation.text: Two sovereigns reach the same dispensing at the same instant, and neither one announces where the other stops mattering. Federal controlled-substance regulation mostly draws an outer boundary: it describes the most a registrant may do without violating federal law, and it does not confer authority to do that thing where the pharmacy actually stands. 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(1) says so in its own text. A Schedule II prescription may be partially filled at a patient's or practitioner's request only if all four of its conditions are met: the partial fill is not prohibited by State law; the prescription is written and filled in accordance with the Act, the federal regulations and State law; the request comes from the patient, a parent or legal guardian of a minor patient, a caregiver of an adult patient named in a medical power of attorney, or the practitioner who wrote the prescription; and the total dispensed across all partial fillings does not exceed the total prescribed. Two of the four point at the state. Read the first exactly: it asks for an absence of state prohibition, not for affirmative state permission, so a jurisdiction that says nothing does not block the partial fill. The second reaches further than it looks, because a prescription that falls short of what State law requires of it has not been written in accordance with State law, and the federal permission is unavailable until that defect is cured.

Now put one patient-requested Schedule II partial fill in front of both sources and take it part by part, because the relationship changes from part to part. Whether the pharmacist dispenses the lesser quantity is a state duty inside a federal permission: federal law permits the partial fill, while under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 18(d3/4) a pharmacist SHALL dispense the lesser quantity if the patient requests it. Where the remaining portion may be dispensed is the same answer under both sovereigns: s. 18(d3/4) allows only the same pharmacy that originally dispensed the lesser quantity to dispense it, and federal law gives a second pharmacy no route either, because 21 CFR 1306.08(e) transfers an electronic prescription only for its initial dispensing, 21 CFR 1306.25 moves only Schedule III-V prescription information for refills, and DEA has stated that no DEA regulation permits a partially filled prescription to be transferred for its remaining portion. What record the dispensing leaves is cumulative: the pharmacist notes that the patient requested the partial fill on a stated date, with the quantity dispensed, and the pharmacy keeps a federal dispensing record for each partial filling, while Massachusetts separately requires a notation of the partial fill and the quantity in the patient's record, accessible to the prescriber on request. Neither record stands in for the other. By when the remaining portion must go out has two matching answers: not later than 30 days after the prescription was written, or 72 hours after issue for an emergency oral prescription, federally, and not later than 30 days after the issue date in Massachusetts.

Other parts of the same transaction are governed by Massachusetts alone. The federal remainder clock in 21 CFR 1306.13(b)(2) times only the remaining portions of a requested partial fill; it does not time the first dispensing. Massachusetts does: under M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 23(a) a written or electronic Schedule II prescription becomes invalid 30 days after the date of issuance, so the first dispensing of an in-state prescription, partial or full, has to fall within those 30 days, counting the day after the prescription was written as day one as 247 CMR 9.04(10) directs. Section 18(d3/4) adds a shorter limit on the initial partial dispensing of a prescription filled pursuant to s. 18(d) or s. 18(d1/2), the two out-of-state routes: not more than 5 days after the issue date. 105 CMR 721.055(A) states the same five-day limit, counted in calendar days, wherever the prescriber's address on the prescription is outside the Commonwealth. And M.G.L. c. 94C, s. 22(c) requires any prescription a practitioner issues for an opioid substance in Schedule II to include a notation that the patient may fill it, upon request, in compliance with s. 18(d3/4), in an amount not exceeding the full prescribed quantity. That duty falls on the prescriber as a matter of what the prescription must contain. It is a different duty from the patient-record notation made at each partial dispensing, and running the two together puts the obligation on the wrong actor. Silence on the federal side is not an argument that any of these points is unregulated.

A different interaction is harder to see, because nothing about it looks like a conflict. Federal law and Massachusetts law each carry a five-refill limit and a six-month limit measured from the issue date, and the two numbers are identical. The scopes are not. 21 CFR 1306.22(a) is addressed to a controlled substance listed in Schedule III or IV: no such prescription may be filled or refilled more than six months after the date it was issued, and none authorised to be refilled may be refilled more than five times. 247 CMR 9.04(13) states the same two limits for Schedule V, and for Schedule V alone. Massachusetts then narrows its own provision by facility rather than by schedule: 247 CMR 9.04(15) provides that the requirements of 247 CMR 9.04(13) do not apply to institutional sterile compounding pharmacies. Storing 'five refills, six months' as a single remembered fact loses all of this. The figure is correct in two places and controlling in neither until the schedule -- and, in Massachusetts, the facility -- is matched to the transaction in front of you.

The working method that survives all of these patterns is the same one. Fix the schedule, the actor, the triggering event, the pathway and the facility before opening any rule. Then take each part of the transaction in turn -- whether it may happen, who must do it, where, by when, and what record it leaves -- and apply every rule, from either sovereign, whose scope actually reaches that part. A federal figure that answers one part, as the 30-day remainder clock answers by when, says nothing about another part, such as where the remainder may be dispensed. Finally, read the stem for which sovereign it is asking about: a stem that names a place rather than a body of law is asking about both.
